findings.description: The RDS instance sets publicly_accessible = true, giving it a public endpoint reachable from the internet. Combined with the exported catalog_db_endpoint output, this significantly increases the attack surface for a database that should only be reachable from the VPC.
storage_encrypted = false disables RDS encryption at rest, so database volumes and snapshots store customer data in cleartext on the underlying storage.

The master password is supplied via var.password and the username is hard-coded to the privileged default 'admin'; the plaintext password is written into Terraform state and is reused directly in EC2 user_data, rather than being sourced from Secrets Manager or manage_master_user_password.

The instance user_data embeds the RDS master username and password in cleartext into /var/www/inc/dbinfo.inc. EC2 user_data is retrievable by anyone with access to the instance metadata service (including via SSRF from the hosted PHP app) and is visible in the console/API, leaking full database admin credentials.

The inline role policy grants s3:*, ec2:* and rds:* on Resource "*". This role is attached via an instance profile to an internet-facing web server, so compromise of the PHP application yields near-administrative control over S3 data, EC2 (including instance/role manipulation for privilege escalation) and all RDS instances.

The bootstrap script installs only plain HTTP (httpd with no TLS configuration) and the MySQL connection is made with mysqli_connect without requiring TLS, so user-submitted data and database traffic traverse the network unencrypted.

No metadata_options block is specified, so IMDSv1 remains enabled. Given the web application on this instance and the highly privileged attached role, an SSRF flaw could be used to retrieve the role's temporary credentials.

skip_final_snapshot = true together with backup_retention_period = 0 means no snapshot protection exists; while partly operational, it also removes the ability to recover data after a destructive attack on the database.

The database security group allows all protocols and ports to 0.0.0.0/0, permitting unrestricted outbound traffic that could be used for data exfiltration or command-and-control from a compromised database host.
